newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania PM says ready to step down if asked.
newsitem.headline: Albania PM says ready to step down if asked.

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi said on Friday he was ready to step down if his ruling Democratic Party asked him to do so, but told party MPs who had demanded his resignation to quit the party if they disagreed with his handling of the current crisis.
"If the party wants my resignation I will agree. Of course I have my own opinions, which I shall make known," he told Reuters in an interview.
He insisted that he still enjoyed the party's full support and said he expected the party's executive committee to declare its support for him at a meeting next week.

Albania has been swept by five weeks of popular unrest since a number of pyramid funds failed, wiping out the life savings of hundreds of thousands of investors, many of whom blame the government for failing to regulate the funds.

Meksi said a petition by 14 Democratic Party MPs asking for his resignation was "nothing new" and those disagreeing with the way he had dealt with the crisis were welcome to leave the parliamentary group.
"They have a right to their opinion and they have the right not to stay with us at this difficult moment," he said.
"I don't have an army of people at my disposal (to allow) me to stay. I am a democrat, I am not Enver Hoxha or a communist," he added.
Meksi said he had been against the spread of pyramid schemes throughout his five-year tenure. "Everybody knows that," he said.
Opposition parties and many Albanians blame President Sali Berisha and Meksi's right-wing government for allowing the schemes to spread and not warning unwary Albanians of their risks.

Albania, Europe's poorest nation, emerged from almost half a century of Stalinist isolation in 1990 when the regime set up by hardline dictator Enver Hoxha accepted opposition parties and began moving towards democracy. Hoxha himself died in 1985.
Violence flared in the capital Tirana on Thursday when riot police prevented some 1,000 anti-government protesters from reaching the main Skanderbeg Square.
Angry protesters and police threw stones, and police then fired volleys of live ammunition in the air to disperse the crowd.
Asked about his reaction to Thursday's events, Meksi said: "They know very well that Tirana is not Vlore. There is no organised crime in Tirana."
He was referring to last week's unrest in the southern town of Vlore, where three people died during violent clashes between police and protesters.
"They want to provoke us. They are speaking for democracy but they are not democrats," Meksi said. "They have the books of Lenin, Marx and Enver Hoxha -- they are for the proletarian revolution."
Meksi was elected for a second term last May after a general election which was widely criticised as unfair.
